paragraphs.title: The Letter to the Babylonian Exiles

easy.explanation: Jeremiah the prophet sent the letter.
easy.q: Who sent the letter?

answers: Only to the king of Babylon
easy.explanation: The letter was sent to those carried away captive to Babylon.
easy.q: To whom was the letter sent?

easy.explanation: Jeremiah sent a letter from Jerusalem.
easy.q: What was sent from Jerusalem?

answers: The elders, priests, prophets, and all the people
medium.explanation: The letter was addressed to several groups among the exiles.
medium.q: Who was included among the recipients of the letter?

medium.explanation: It was sent by Elasah and Gemariah.
medium.q: By whose hand was the letter sent?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the people being taken from Jerusalem to Babylon.
medium.q: What does “carried away captive” mean in this passage?

answers: The message was intended for the whole exiled community
The message was secret and only for the king
The message was intended only for the messengers
challenge.explanation: The many recipients show that the letter addressed the entire exiled society.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the letter being sent to the elders, priests, prophets, and all the people?

challenge.explanation: The letter was sent by their hand.
challenge.q: What was the role of Elasah and Gemariah?

answers: Zedekiah sent them to the king of Babylon
Zedekiah received the letter from them
challenge.explanation: Zedekiah sent them to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.
challenge.q: What connection is described between Zedekiah and the messengers?

paragraphs.title: Settled Life and Welfare in Exile

easy.explanation: They were commanded to build houses and dwell in them.
easy.q: What were the exiles commanded to build?

answers: Plant them and eat their fruit
easy.explanation: They were told to plant gardens and eat the fruit of them.
easy.q: What were the exiles commanded to do with gardens?

easy.explanation: They were to seek the peace of the city where they had been carried.
easy.q: For whom were they to seek peace?

answers: Build, dwell, plant, and establish families
medium.explanation: The commands describe stable family, agricultural, and community life.
medium.q: Which sequence describes the exiles’ life?

answers: Because its peace would give them peace
Because the city would immediately return them
Because they were required to fight
medium.explanation: The verse connects the peace of the city with their own peace.
medium.q: Why were the exiles to pray for the city?

answers: People who claim to reveal the future
medium.explanation: Diviners are people who claim supernatural knowledge of the future.
medium.q: In the KJV, what are “diviners”?

answers: It was expected to last a long time
It would end that same day
challenge.explanation: The command fits a prolonged period of life in exile.
challenge.q: What does the command to establish families and multiply suggest about the length of the exile?

answers: Their welfare was connected to the welfare of the place where they lived
The exiles had no connection with the city
The city had to leave Babylon
challenge.explanation: The verse says that in the city’s peace they would have peace.
challenge.q: What is the connection between seeking the city’s peace and the exiles’ lives?

answers: They prophesied falsely in God’s name
challenge.explanation: The LORD said those prophets had not been sent.
challenge.q: Why did Jeremiah warn the exiles not to believe the prophets and diviners?

easy.explanation: The passage speaks of seventy years being completed at Babylon.
easy.q: How many years would pass before God visited the exiles?

answers: Bring the people back to that place
easy.explanation: The LORD promised to cause them to return.
easy.q: What did the LORD promise to do afterward?

answers: Thoughts of peace and not of evil
easy.explanation: The LORD said His thoughts were of peace and an expected end.
easy.q: What were the LORD’s thoughts toward the people?

medium.explanation: They would call upon the LORD and pray unto Him.
medium.q: What would the exiles do so that the LORD would hear them?

answers: Seeking Him with all their heart
medium.explanation: The passage says they would find Him when they searched for Him with all their heart.
medium.q: What was required for them to find the LORD?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the hopeful future God intended for His people.
medium.q: What does “an expected end” mean in this context?

answers: They mention seventy years but promise a return
They deny any possibility of return
challenge.explanation: The exile would be long, but it would not be the end of the people.
challenge.q: How do these verses combine a long exile with hope?

answers: They call, pray, seek, and find
challenge.explanation: The verses describe sincere prayer and seeking God.
challenge.q: What sequence is described concerning the people’s prayer?

answers: Gathering the people from all places and bringing them back
The return of only a few individuals
challenge.explanation: The LORD promised to gather them from all nations and places and bring them back.
challenge.q: What does the promised return include?

paragraphs.title: The Fate of Those Remaining in Jerusalem

answers: That the people would return quickly
That the exile would last seventy years
That the prophets would be punished
easy.explanation: The people said that the LORD had raised up prophets in Babylon.
easy.q: What did the prophets in Babylon claim?

answers: The king and the people who had not gone into captivity
easy.explanation: The passage speaks of their brethren who had not gone into captivity.
easy.q: Who remained in Jerusalem according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The LORD said He would send sword, famine, and pestilence.
easy.q: What judgments would come upon those remaining?

answers: The exiles received a promise of return, while the others faced judgment
The exiles were immediately punished, while the others returned
medium.explanation: The passage presents different destinies for the two groups.
medium.q: What contrast is made between the exiles and those remaining in Jerusalem?

answers: As vile figs that cannot be eaten
medium.explanation: They are compared to figs so evil that they cannot be eaten.
medium.q: How are those remaining in Jerusalem described through the image of figs?

medium.explanation: The words describe shame and rejection among the nations.
medium.q: What does “a curse, and an astonishment, and an hissing, and a reproach” describe?

answers: Their promise of a quick return was false
They commanded the exiles to build houses
challenge.explanation: Those prophets contradicted the LORD’s message about the long exile.
challenge.q: Why did Jeremiah warn the exiles not to believe the prophets in Babylon?

answers: They did not hearken to the LORD’s words and prophets
challenge.explanation: The LORD said they had not listened to His words delivered by His prophets.
challenge.q: What explicit reason is given for the judgment on those remaining?

answers: A promise of peace and return versus sword, famine, and pestilence
challenge.explanation: The passage sets two sharply different destinies against each other.
challenge.q: What literary device creates the contrast between the exiles and those remaining?

answers: Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah
easy.explanation: These are the two prophets whom the LORD condemned.
easy.q: Who were the two prophets named in these verses?

answers: Only about the peace of Jerusalem
easy.explanation: They prophesied falsely in the LORD’s name.
easy.q: What did the two men prophesy?

answers: Slay them before the people’s eyes
easy.explanation: The LORD said He would deliver them into Nebuchadrezzar’s hand, and he would slay them.
easy.q: What would Nebuchadrezzar do to the two prophets?

answers: Adultery and speaking falsely in God’s name
medium.explanation: The passage mentions adultery and false words spoken in the LORD’s name.
medium.q: What other acts were attributed to these prophets?

medium.explanation: Their names would be used in a curse among the captivity of Judah.
medium.q: What would their fate become among the exiles?

medium.explanation: Villany means a disgraceful or wicked act.
medium.q: What does “villany” mean in this passage?

answers: They combined false prophecy with serious immoral conduct
They merely confused the name of the city
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes both their lies and their adultery.
challenge.q: Why was the punishment of these prophets fitting for their actions?

answers: The LORD knows their deeds and bears witness against them
The king is the only witness
challenge.explanation: The LORD presents Himself as fully aware of their actions.
challenge.q: What is conveyed by “I know, and am a witness”?

answers: Their names would be remembered as examples of severe judgment
They would become leaders of the exiles
challenge.explanation: Their names would be used as a formula expressing judgment.
challenge.q: What does turning their fate into a curse signify?

easy.explanation: Shemaiah sent letters in his own name.
easy.q: Who sent letters against Jeremiah?

easy.explanation: Shemaiah addressed Zephaniah the priest.
easy.q: To whom did Shemaiah appeal for action?

answers: He read it in Jeremiah’s ears
He sent it to the king
easy.explanation: Zephaniah read the letter aloud to Jeremiah.
easy.q: What did Zephaniah do with the letter?

medium.explanation: Shemaiah urged Zephaniah to reprove and restrain Jeremiah.
medium.q: What did Shemaiah demand that Zephaniah do?

answers: An officer over those who were mad and made themselves prophets
A messenger to the king of Babylon
medium.explanation: The letter refers to Zephaniah’s authority over such people.
medium.q: What position did Zephaniah hold in the house of the LORD?

answers: An instrument or place of punishment and confinement
medium.explanation: The stocks were used to restrain or punish a person.
medium.q: What does “the stocks” refer to in this context?

answers: He did not fulfill Shemaiah’s demand
He agreed to cast Jeremiah out
challenge.explanation: The text records that he read the letter but does not say that he acted against Jeremiah.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Zephaniah reading the letter but not acting against Jeremiah?

answers: Shemaiah opposed Jeremiah’s message that the captivity would be long
challenge.explanation: Shemaiah objected to Jeremiah’s teaching that the captivity would last a long time.
challenge.q: What was the source of the conflict between Shemaiah and Jeremiah?

answers: As a prophet who should be reproved and restrained
challenge.explanation: Shemaiah treated Jeremiah as someone who should be opposed for his prophecy.
challenge.q: How does Shemaiah’s letter portray Jeremiah?

paragraphs.title: The Judgment of Shemaiah the Nehelamite

easy.explanation: The message was to be sent to all those in captivity.
easy.q: To whom did the LORD command Jeremiah to send the message?

easy.explanation: Shemaiah prophesied even though the LORD had not sent him.
easy.q: What did Shemaiah do without being sent by the LORD?

easy.explanation: The passage names Shemaiah and his seed as subject to punishment.
easy.q: Who would be punished with Shemaiah?

answers: It caused them to trust in a lie
It caused them to plant gardens
medium.explanation: The LORD said Shemaiah caused the people to trust in a lie.
medium.q: What effect did Shemaiah’s prophecy have on the people?

answers: The good the LORD would do for His people
medium.explanation: He would not behold the future good promised to the people.
medium.q: What would Shemaiah not see?

answers: He taught opposition or disobedience against the LORD
medium.explanation: The phrase describes leading people into rebellion against God.
medium.q: What does “he hath taught rebellion” mean in this context?

answers: He would not live to see the fulfillment of that promise
challenge.explanation: Part of his punishment was that he would not behold the good God would do.
challenge.q: Why is Shemaiah’s judgment connected with the future good promised to the people?

answers: The LORD announced waiting and return, while Shemaiah gave false confidence
challenge.explanation: Shemaiah contradicted the LORD’s message about the prolonged captivity.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the LORD’s message and Shemaiah’s message?

answers: So all the exiles would know that Shemaiah’s prophecy was not from the LORD
So Shemaiah could be made their leader
So the people would be told to build houses
challenge.explanation: The judgment exposed Shemaiah’s false message to the whole community.
challenge.q: Why was the announcement sent to all the captivity?

paragraphs.title: Summary of the Message to the Exiles

answers: To settle in exile and seek the peace of the city
easy.explanation: The exiles were told to live, multiply, and seek the city’s peace.
easy.q: What is the central message given to the exiles in this chapter?

easy.explanation: The LORD promised to gather and bring the exiles back.
easy.q: What did the LORD promise after seventy years?

easy.explanation: The exiles were warned not to listen to false prophecies.
easy.q: What warning did Jeremiah give concerning false prophets?

answers: The exiles were to live there for a long time while still expecting a future return
Life in exile canceled the promise of return
medium.explanation: The chapter joins faithful life in the present with hope for the future.
medium.q: How are settled life in exile and the promise of return related?

answers: Because in its peace they would have peace
Because the city would immediately free them
Because they were forbidden to pray
medium.explanation: This is the reason explicitly given in the passage.
medium.q: Why were the exiles to seek the peace of the city?

answers: People carried away from their homeland
The army of the king of Babylon
medium.explanation: It refers to the people who had been taken from their land into exile.
medium.q: What does “captivity” mean in the context of this chapter?

answers: They must live faithfully in exile while maintaining hope of return
They must choose between prayer and family
They must decide whether to build or destroy
challenge.explanation: The chapter calls them to adapt to the present while trusting God’s future promise.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in Jeremiah’s message to the exiles?

answers: A true prophet is sent by the LORD, while a false prophet speaks without being sent
A true prophet lives only in Jerusalem
A false prophet always speaks about peace
challenge.explanation: Being sent by the LORD is a central test in the chapter.
challenge.q: How does the chapter distinguish a true prophet from a false prophet?

answers: A letter to the exiles, instructions for life, a promise of return, and condemnation of false prophets
War, victory, Temple building, and return
Return, exile, a letter, and punishment
challenge.explanation: This sequence follows the chapter’s principal movement.
challenge.q: What is the main sequence of ideas in the chapter?
